hepatic.value: Contraindicated in acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis. Chronic alcoholic liver disease modestly increases exposure (Child-Pugh A: Cmax +60%, AUC +5%; Child-Pugh B: Cmax +100%, AUC +21%).

In patients with Child‑Pugh A disease, C max and AUC were increased by 60% and 5%, respectively, as compared with patients with normal liver function. In patients with Child‑Pugh B disease, C max and AUC were increased 100% and 21%, respectively, compared with patients with normal liver function.
There have been rare reports of new-onset or exacerbation of myasthenia gravis, including ocular myasthenia, and reports of recurrence when the same or a different statin was administered.

refs.quote: Rosuvastatin is a substrate of CYP2C9 and transporters (such as OATP1B1, BCRP). Rosuvastatin plasma levels can be significantly increased with concomitant administration of inhibitors of CYP2C9 and transporters.

value.effect: Significantly increases rosuvastatin plasma levels (up to 7.4-fold AUC), increasing risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

tier.note: PLLR Pregnancy section explicitly states 'Discontinue CRESTOR when pregnancy is recognized' because rosuvastatin decreases synthesis of cholesterol and biologically active cholesterol derivatives and may cause fetal harm, while treatment of hypercholesterolemia is generally unnecessary during pregnancy. (Although a Medicaid cohort of 1,152 statin-exposed pregnancies showed adjusted RR 1.07 for malformations, label directs discontinuation).

refs.quote: Discontinue CRESTOR when pregnancy is recognized. Alternatively, consider the ongoing therapeutic needs of the individual patient. CRESTOR decreases synthesis of cholesterol and possibly other biologically active substances derived from cholesterol; therefore, CRESTOR may cause fetal harm when administered to pregnant patients based on the mechanism of action
